Sensational Episode at West Point—A Plucky California Girl.

New York, August 25th.—A somewhat sensational episode is reported to have occurred at Cranston's Hotel, West Point, last night. The story is that a young man calling himself Captain Bursel, and representing himself as an officer in the British army, arrived at the hotel three weeks ago, and registered as from "Windsor Palace, England." He had brought a letter of introduction from Grace Greenwood to President Garfield, and made many friends in New York among the Wall-street brokers, by whom he had been introduced at the Union Club. At the hotel he met a Miss Scofie of San Francisco, and the daughter of a mine-owner, who was sojourning at West Point with her mother. A few morning since Bursel, it is stated, in conversation with Miss Scofie, informed the young lady point blank that she lied, and she at once laid the case before the manager of the house, with the statement that a person possessing such characteristics should not be tolerated by the guests. Bursel, however, was too intimate with the hotel proprietors, and too firmly supported by the male guests, to permit his being turned away. Last evening Miss Scofie went with her mother to a cadet hop, and as they were ascending the steps leading to the verandah, the young lady met Bursel, who was leaning against a post smoking. As she attempted to pass, he blew a cloud of smoke into her face, and quickly followed it up with another, at the same time smiling at her discomfiture. Miss Scofie appealed to the bystanders for protection, but none being offered she struck the alleged Captain full in the face, knocking his cigar out of his mouth. She followed this up with a second blow with her fist. Bursel raised his hand, containing a cane, to ward off the blows, when she caught the stick, wrenched it from his grasp, and boiling with rage struck him squarely in the face several times, cutting him badly. The Captain, who has a false leg, was thrown to the piazza in the melee. Mixed Poll Ics.

JACKSON (Miss.), August 25th.—The Republicans to-day ratified the Greenback nomination and agreed on a fusion ticket, with Ben King for Governor, S. J. Yellowby for Lieutenant-Governor, S. K. Shellman (colored) for Secretary of State, W. H. Bynam for Treasurer, A. T. Wimberly for Attorney-General, W. D. House for Superintendent of Education. A joint mass meeting was held to-night, presided over by John R. Lynch (colored).

Daring Robbery in Missouri.

ST. LOUIS, August 25th.—The Republican's Lexington, Mo., special says: An omnibus which was conveying passengers from the Wabash Railroad to Lexington, about 8 o'clock this evening, was entered by four heavily-armed and marked men, who robbed the passengers—five in number—of all their money, watches and other valuables and then escaped. A posse of men have gone in pursuit of the robbers.

Murder in Colorado—Lynchers Searching for the Murderer.

DENVER (Col.), August 25th.—The News' South Arkansas special says: The body of a man named McCorkey was found at Mears last night. The evidence points strongly to Charles Stone, a notorious desperado, as the murderer. Stone came over to South Arkansas shortly after the murder, and was arrested en route. A number of McCorkey's friends came after him, but the officials spirited him away. Fifty armed men are to-night scouring the streets looking for the murderer, with the intention of lynching him!

The Drought in Kentucky.

LOUISVILLE, August 25th.—The city is flooded with stock. Countrymen are bringing them in rather than feed them at great loss. They must haul corn from the city for feed if they keep the usual number. There has been little rain in the usual number. There has been little corn is destroyed and the late crop badly damaged.

Man and Wife Killed by Lightning.
CHICAGO, August 25th.—A man and wife named Temple were instantly killed in their house by a lightning stroke near Fulton, Ill., early this morning. Their five little children, who were in the house with them, miraculously escaped uninjured.

Death of an Ex-Congressman.
FREDERICKSburg (Va.), August 25th.—Daniel C. Dejarnette, a member of the Thirty-sixth Congress, and afterwards in the Confederate House of Representatives from the Richmond district, is dead.

Mining Case Decided.
WASHINGTON, August 25th.—Hon. N. C. McFarland, Commissioner of the General Land Office, to-day decided the case of the Bodie Tunnel Company vs the Tioga and Bechtel Mining Companies of California, in favor of the latter companies.

Murder at Mears.
On last Wednesday night a foul murder was committed at the littie town of Mears, Colorado, on the D. & R. G. road some six miles above Poncho Springs, on the person of Edward McClarkey, who it is said has two brothers living at, or near Gunnison City, and whose parents live somewhere near Leavenworth, Kansas.

McClarkey was serving as teamster for the Hudson Constructing company, of the D. & R. G. Railway Co., and had the reputation of being a steady quiet hard working man.

At the coroner's inquest very little testimony was elicited, as to the probable cause of death, owing to the fact, that no examination of the body was made until after the witnesses had been discharged, when it was discovered on stripping the body that McClarkey had been fatally shot through, or in the region of the heart, the bullet being found after passing through the body, in his undershirt.

Suspicion very naturally fell on a few notorious characters who have infested the place for several months, two miscrable women by the name C. A. Powers and Lizzie Wendall, alias Spurgeon and two villianous men by the name of Charles Coun and Charley Stone. On the arrival of the eastern train all four of those suspected characters, hastly boarded the train, and got off before it was known in time to capture them, but an extra train was soon put in motion, and the parties were overhauled at Salida, and this morning were taken to the Buena Vista jail. Conn and Stone were desperate characters and the community at Mears are rejoiced at their departure.

To-day in the bagnio occupied by these women, at Mears, there was a spontaneous combustion, and despite the efforts of the citizens, the entire building with its contents were consumed by fire.

The body of McClarkey was buried to-day above the little town of Mears. About one hundred turned out and followed the remaines to its last resting place.

MEARS, COLO., Aug. 27, 1881.

There are at least two thousand farmers in Anderson county who have given liens this year to secure advances with which to make their crop, and if the law is repealed this winter what will they do next year? It is fair to presume that only those who cannot obtain supplies without liens give them, and why any one should desire to deprive them of its friendly aid is more than we can understand.

Public opinion in this county, as in every other section of the State, is divided on the question of the lien law, but we do not believe the clamorings for its repeal are so general as elsewhere. We believe the repealing of the law at the next session of the Legislature, on the heels of the general failure of the crops, would be a calamity from which the State would not recover for years to come. Let the law stand as it is. It is a necessity to the agricultural interests of the whole State. What would become of the thousands of poor farmers, both white and colored, who now obtain their advances under its provisions?

Mr. E. F. Stokes, counsel for Dodson, Burton, Adams and Bates, the Greenville incendiaries sentenced to be hanged on the 9th of September, has filed the necessary papers for an appeal with the Clerk of the Supreme Court. This would operate to stay the execution, but Mr. Stokes will probably obtain an order restraining the Sheriff from executing the sentence of the Court from one of the Justices. The Supreme Court will not meet until November, and even if the new trial asked for is not granted, the prisoners will have to be re-sentenced. He is one of the most valuable members of the Board of Agriculture, and with a most genial and cultivated, though unassuming, gentleman. We were pleased to see him in our midst, and are gratified to learn that he carried with him favorable impressions of our county and its progress.

The gentlemen who composed the Council that went out of office on Monday last have made a good record for themselves. They have discharged their duties in a most acceptable manner, and leave several public improvements to testify for years to come to come to their efficiency, progressiveness and public spiritedness. They deserve the "well done" of all our citizens, whom they have earnestly striven to serve satisfactorily. Mr. Tolly, the retiring Intendant, had been in service for three years consecutively, and always took great interest in whatever affected the welfare of the town, and never neglected any of the various duties devolving upon him. Mr. Murrah, the senior Warden, had served the town four years in succession, and was always at his post of duty, and allowed no other consideration than the welfare of his constituency to govern him in any of his acts. Wardens Maxwell and Taylor, though in the Council for only one year, showed their peculiar fitness for the positions they held in many ways. Their judgment upon all matters was mature, and was always at his post of duty, and allowed no other consideration than the welfare of his constituency to govern him in any of his acts. The fifth member of the old Council, Mr. Payne, is also a member of the present Council, and his re-election is the best testimony that could be given of the esteem in which he is held by the citizens of the town. Whatever adverse criticisms may be passed upon any of the acts of the outgoing Council, taken singly, none can deny that they have done their duty well, and that they deserve the hearty thanks of all our people.

The Fort Gaines Tribune chronicles the death of two prominent citizens—Mr. J. R. M. Sanders and Mr. Fielding Rambo, at Bluffton.

The English Manufacturing Company will send skilled operatives to demonstrate what their machinery is capable of. This will put the American and European machinery in direct competition.

LaGrange is preparing for a larger trade this fall than ever before.

There are only three inmates in the Troup county jail at present, and one of them is a lunatic.

McVille, Telfair county, wants a blacksmith.

TRIPLE MURDER.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

ATLANTA, Ga., Aug. 10.—Near Dawson, in Terrell County, yesterday was enacted a triple murder, the motive of which was robbery. The details appear to be that a negro named Frank Hudson called at the house of an old white man named David Lee, who it was known kept a good sum of money in his house. Fluding Lee at home, with a view of decoying him away from the house, he told him that his field fence, a short distance from his residence, was on fire. Lee started for the scene, accompanied by Hudson, who offered, to assist him in putting out the flames. The negro, before going, picked up an ax, stating he would probably need it to cut away the burning portion. Soon after leaving the house and while on the way to the place where the fence was said to be burning, Hudson struck Lee a terrible blow on the head with the ax, splitting his head open and killing him instantly. He then returned to the house, when he killed Mrs. Lee and servant with the same ax, and also struck down with the same weapon another servant girl, leaving her as he supposed in a dying condition. Hudson then robbed the house, getting $500 as the proceeds of his fledglish crime, and left. An hour later a neighbor called and found the fourth victim of Hudson in a recovering condition, and she detailed what had occurred, and soon the entire neighborhood was alarmed and out in search of Hudson, who, if captured, will be lynched.

PROBABLY LYNCHED.
ATLANTA, Ga., Aug. 20.—Your correspondent yesterday telegraphed the details then at hand relative to the brutal murder of David Lee and wife, two old and respectable citizens of Terrell County, and also the killing of a negro woman and the probably fatal wounding of another negro woman by Frank Hudson (colored), who committed the crime for the purpose of robbing the Lees' residence and leaving no living witnesses to tell the tale. Hudson, after committing the crime, fled and was pursued by Sherid Edwards, of Dougherty County, and Marshal Westbrook, two of the best detectives in that section of the State. He was overhauled on Bates' plantation, in Lee County, and taken to Albany, where he was landed in jail. The fact that the murder was of a most unprovoked character, and that he had killed both white and colored people, carried the indignation of both races wild, both together assuming a formidable shape. The indignation was so strong that considerable fears were entertained for the safety of Hudson by the authorities. The Guards were called out by Mayor Wilder, but refused to respond, giving as an excuse that the Mayor had no authority to call out the military. It is said that this would not have stopped them bad they any desire to protect the negro, but that public sentiment was so strongly in favor of lynch law that they did not care to interfere and prevent it being administered. The Governor was telegraphed by the Sherif, asking him to authorize the Albany Guards to turn out and guard the jail for the purpose of protecting the life of Hudson, but, as the Governor was out of the city, there was no one to act in his place, and it is believed here that ere this Hudson has been lynched. If this be so, no effort will be made to bring the lynchers before the courts, as public sentiment will crush such a thing out.

PITTSBURG, Aug. 20.—At the hearing in the Mollie Maguires murder case at Union-town to-day four witnesses were examined, the most important being William McDowell and Robert Long. McDowell testified to being present at the license hearing in Dunbar on June 11, when there were present also Healy, Kane, and Collins. The latter presented McFarland's license petition to McDowell with the request to sign it, which was refused. He then asked Healy to sign it, who also refused, telling him to go away with his whisky gang. Hot words ensued, and Healy withdrew. Collins again approached McDowell, who to get rid of him said: "Get Healy to sign it and then I will." and Collins replied, "God damn him, he'll be attended to." Kane then stepped up and added: "Yes, as soon as this license question is settled, you — — —, he'll be attended to." Robert King deposed that while returning from the dedication of a Catholic church in Scottdale about the 1st of June, he and Healy were approached by Kane in the cars. Kane said to Healy: "If you try to ruin me and my family I'll whip the head off of you, by God! I mean to do it." The testimony of Ella Casey and John Bunting was unimportant, except to establish the presence of Rogan, McFarland, Flood, the two Dolans, and two unrecognized men in the neighborhood of the murder. This closed the hearing. After a review of the testimony, respective counsel, the Court decided that Martin Donohoe be discharged, that John Kane be remanded, and that the rest be admitted to bail, as follows: James McFarland and Pat Dolan in the sum of $5,000 each, John Collins in $3,000, and Mike Dolan, Bernard Flood, and James Rogan in $500 each. According to an account given by the Albany News, Frank Hudson, alias Arthur Wade, the negro murderer of the Lee family in Terrell county, had a stormy trip to and reception at Dawson after his arrest in Lee county. Every station along the road was crowded with excited people endeavoring to see the prisoner, but he was locked securely in one of the cars. At Brown's station twenty-five or thirty men from Terrell entered the cars, but did not see the prisoner. At Dawson he was taken out and literally borne away by one thousand five hundred or two thousand persons of both colors, equally bent on his immediate execution, to the court house, where he was thrown from the doorway to the ground and finally placed on a table to narrate the horrors of the butchery. Hargrove drew his pistol, and McKnight and Ezell both leaped from the wagon and Hargrove fired on them. The ball passed through McKnight's coat. He then fired at Ezell. ORIGIN OF THE DIFFICULTY.
One account furnished us states that the riot originated in the following manner: On Saturday the 13th instant a young man named Coulbourn was passing Dana's marine railway when he asked a colored man in Dana's employ, at work in a scow, to do him a favor, but Dana objected and Coulbourn boarded the scow to thrash the man for refusing. The colored man got the advantage and several of Coulbourn's friends started to his aid in a skiff; on seeing which the colored man, though unable to swim, jumped overboard. A peaceable and industrious colored man started to the assistance of the drowning man who was however rescued when nearly drowned by the party in the skiff. A few words passed between the crowd and Tucker, but the latter went away to his work. On last Friday night a party of white men who had been drinking freely was standing in front of Blizzard's bebaving in a disorderly manner, when Tucker passed by. According to reliable eye witnesses, John Holland said to him, Tucker, you d—s—of a b—you'll not stay here long. Tucker foolishly stopped to argue the point when he received heavy blows on the head with some hard weapon. He put his hand to his head and ran saying "Oh my God! I'm nearly murdered.—Rumor says George Holland ran after him to the corner of the alley and stood behind a new house and then with his right hand, head and neck in the alley fired several shots down the alley. While so shooting the shots were returned by some unknown and invisible person from an upstairs window, probably, when Holland was seriously wounded. The alley is inhabited by a number of colored folks. The above account appears to be the origin of the greatly to-be-regretted affair which led to another out-break on Saturday night. At last accounts the town was very much excited, but precaution was taken to prevent further disturbance.—Somerset Herald.

LINCOLN, Neb., July 6.—The Fourth passed off in this city with a horrible accident and two or three serious stabbing and shooting affrays. AN OVERDOSE OF OPIUM.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

MILWAUKEE, July 6.—Ida Alb, a female wrestler in Adam Forepaugh's circus, who was compelled to lay over in this city on account of ill-health several weeks since, and has been in the hospital ever since, accidentally took an overdose of opium this afternoon, from the effects of which she soon died.

KILLED IN A HARVEST-FIELD.
MOUNT STERLING, Ky., July 6.—Honey Allen, colored, was killed yesterday in a harvest-field eight miles from here by Dick Freeman. Allen had refused to work, and threatened Freeman, when the latter cut his throat. Parties were at Allen's house last night to lynch him for an assault upon a woman, but found him already dead.

A FATAL FALL.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
MILWAUKEE, July 6.—A stovedore named Rich, while engaged in unloading old iron from the Canadian schooner Alaconis to-day, fell into the vessel's hold and sustained fatal injuries.

SIXTY PERSONS POISONED.
Norwich, Conn., July 6.—At a picnic party near here on the 4th, sixty persons were poisoned by coffee prepared in a copper boiler. No deaths.

PAUPERS.

The Indianapolis Poor-Farm Investigation Still in Progress—Evidence for the Defense.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., July 6.—The Poor-Farm investigation still drags its slow length along, notwithstanding the excessive heat of the past few days. The defense scored some good points to-day, introducing a number of prominent business-men who have supplied the institution with meat, bread, and provisions, who uniformly testified that the articles furnished, while not always the highest in price, were sound and good. A number of witnesses were introduced to prove the good character of Superintendent Wright for peace, quiet, and humanity, and to show that the asylum was clean and well kept, and the inmates properly cared for. Ilbram W. Waller, Trustee of Wayne Township, while testifying to the peaceable character of Wright, admitted on cross-examination that he thought Wright had been more severe in his discipline than his predecessor. The defense say they have a large number of witnesses yet to call, and that the evidence will take until the end of the week.

AN INTERRUPTED BREAKFAST.
A Party of Mexicans Baset With Cowboys and Robbed of $4,000 and Mules-Four of the Mexicans Missing.
Report comes to us of a fresh outrage perpetrated by the cowboys in Sonora. Early last Monday morning a party of sixteen Mexicans from the interior of Sonora on their way to this Territory to purchase goods and carrying $4,000 for that purpose, stopped at a curve in the road at Los Animas, near Fronteras, to prepare their frugal breakfast. While busily engaged preparing their tortillas they were saluted with the music of twenty rifles fired by cowboys who lay in ambush awaiting them. The Mexicans took this as invitation to leave and did not stand on the order of their going but left all their mules and pack saddles in which they carried their money for the purchase of goods. When they stopped running they were at Fronteras and their party was four short. The missing men are supposed to have been killed. The citizens of Babispe and troops are after the cowboys and are disposed to take summary vengeance if they overtake them.—Tuscon Citizen.

Ten of the men injured in the explosion at the Woolner distillery, Peorfa, Ill., have died. Only four of the eighteen who were exposed to the shock are expected to recover. The Coroner's jury found a verdict to the effect that the explosion was caused by too great a pressure of steam in the still.

While Miss Mary Gerhardt, aged 18, was crossing Scalp's Mountain, five miles north of Port Clinton, a rough-looking man jumped out from the bush and seized Miss Gerhardt, who struggled desperately to free herself from his grasp and succeeded after breaking her parasol over his head. The news of the attempted outrage soon spread and a party started in pursuit and found the man in the woods near Pine Grove. Preparations were made to lynch the villain, but his pleadings for mercy saved him, and he was sent to jail.

A true bill has been found against William T. Phelan, alias George D. Healey, the noted one armed forger, who swindled the bank at Emlenton out of five hundred dollars some months ago. He forged drafts on banks in Oil City, Clarion county, in Illinois and several other places. He has been arrested two or three times, but each time broke jail or escaped in some way. Once he jumped from a train while it was in rapid motion and escaped. He was arrested a few days since in Kansas, and on his way East offered the sheriff five hundred dollars if he would let him go.

He was lying on a lounge before a fire place and under the mantel-piece. The lightning entered a flue, passed through a stovepipe, struck the lounge, tearing out a piece nearly its entire length, and pitched Mr. Orton some distance into the room.... Capt. J. C. Weaks left here last Friday for Shreveport to enter upon his duties as U. S. Marshal for the Western District of Louisiana.... Last Tuesday, in the tenth ward, a colored man shot and dangerously wounded Mr. Scott Lanier, with whom he had previously had a difficulty. The Negro fired four shots at Mr. Lanier, twice with a shot gun and twice with a pistol, eight bullets striking Lanier. As soon as he committed the feud the Negro fled, but was pursued by the Constable and a posse. He was overtaken Tuesday night, and refusing to surrender, was fired upon and fatally wounded. Another Negro, charged with being accessory to the shooting of Lanier, was arrested and lodged in jail by the Constable.

The people of Minden are making vigorous efforts to have the line of Vicksburg, Shreveport and Pacific Railway so changed that it will pass through their town.

Gretna Courier: There was a meeting of citizens Tuesday evening for the purpose of protesting against the right of the Pacific Railway to lay its track along Third street.

Webster Tribune: Whooping cough of a malignant type is still prevailing in Minden. It has been quite fatal among the colored children. For the past two months three or four a week have died from this malady.

St. Charles Herald: Wednesday morning, rice cutting began in rear of Hahnville. The day was marked with many casualties, as it is reported some fifteen or twenty hands were overcome by the heat and fainted in the fields.

Clinton Patriot Democrat: Maria Thorton, an aged colored women, received from the hands of her daughter, Laura Morrison, a dose of morphia in lieu of quinine, causing death from the sad mistake a few moments afterwards.

Madison Journal: A shooting scrape occurred Monday evening, back of Omega, between Mr. James Gilfoil and his brother-in-law, Mr. Perry. Both parties were shot, the former in the arm and the latter in the mouth. Neither shot will likely prove fatal.

Iberia Journal: It is decided that a branch railroad will be built from Jeanerette to Cypremst., although not largely attended on account of the inclementy of the weather, $8250 was subscribed for the building of the road.

Robert Hill, a colored man who killed his brother on the plantation of Mr. Wm. L. Shaffer, in Terrebonne parish, some months ago, was recently arrested in Vicksburg on a requisition from Gov. Wiltz, and has been returned to Terrebonne to stand his trial.

Lafayette Advertiser: A rumor to the effect that the convicts in camp above Washington had revolted, killed the guards and made their escape was generally current a few days since, and created some consternation. It subsequently proved to be without foundation.

St. Landry Democrat: There is a woman in this parish who gave birth to four children at one time, two boys and two girls, all living and old enough to walk. Another St. Landry woman has had sixteen children in sixteen years—twins twice—ten of whom are now living. This beats immigration.

Morehouse Cotton Plant: A colored man named Harrison Lyons, Jr., while loading his gun accidentally discharged it, the load of squirrel shot entering his abdomen and wounded him mortally.

The Negro that shot Mr. Scott Lanier some time since, and whom the constable's posse shot in capturing him, had his arm amputated. Gangrene having set in the physicians think another amputation must be made. Mr. Lanier has recovered from his wounds.

St. John Meschacebe: The Bonnet Carré crevasse is a shame to lower Louisiana and should not have been permitted to run so long to the prejudice of a fertile region of the State and our important lakes. A subscription sufficient to defray the expense of building a permanent levee is proposed. In a letter to the Democrat, Mr B. Laplace, our worthy citizen, offers to start the list with a contribution of $1000.

Morehouse Clarion: Wesley Frazier and Joe Williams, two colored men, became involved in a difficulty on the Wilderness place, which resulted in the latter being shot by Frazier. The weapon used was a double-barrel shot gun, thirty buckshot entering the body of Williams. He lived about twelve hours after being shot. From what we have heard of the affair Frazier's provocation to shoot Williams was great. Frazier surrendered to the officers of the law.

Madison Journal: We are informed that work will soon begin in earnest all along the line of the V. S. & P. R. R. Raising the road bed between this place and Monroe, building the bridge across the Onachita river and completing the gap between Monroe and Shreveport will be carried on simultaneously. Mr. Preston Hawkans, a native of Madison and a young man of promise, was accidentally drowned while bathing in the river on the 9th instant.
